scenario: AITA For Selling My Former Roommates Games | So a few years ago I was renting this place with this dude and we were on a lease. When the lease was nearing it's end he just peaced out. We're talking took most of everything leaving only the last bit of his half of rent and a few things he said in a note he didn't want to bring with him. Thing with where I live is that if you don't discard of things on your own when you move out the landlord can pay to have someone remove the stuff. We're talking cases of dudes having $250 taken off their deposit just for some dude to take 3 milk crates of things to the dump. It's a rip off. I texted and emailed him for 2 weeks asking to pick these things up or take them to the dump but he never responded. So I took most of his things to the dump but he also had around 60 video games for PS4. So I figured I'd sell them. There is a local game store where they buy used games and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Well cut to last week and I was at a party he was at and we were polite. He then asks how the move out was and I said good, and naturally he asked what I did with his stuff. He got mad when he found out I sold his games but I told him that I tried to get him to grab these things but he never reached out. He's now calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked and legally there's nothing there but now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

So, the person was renting a place with a roommate, and when the lease was ending, the roommate just left without taking most of his stuff. He left a note saying he didn't want to bring a few things with him. The landlord in this area can charge tenants if they don't remove their belongings, which can be expensive—like $250 taken from a deposit for just a few milk crates of stuff. That's pretty rip-off.

The person tried to contact the former roommate for two weeks, texting and emailing, asking him to pick up his things or take them to the dump, but he never responded. So, the person took most of the roommate's stuff to the dump. However, the roommate had around 60 video games for the PS4. Instead of taking them to the dump, the person decided to sell them. He went to a local game store, sold all the games, and got $600.

Then, at a party, the roommate found out about this. He got mad when he heard that his games were sold. The person explained that he tried to contact him but didn't get a response, so he sold the games. Now, the roommate is calling him an asshole and asking for the money back. The person checked legally, and there's nothing he can do, but he's wondering if he's the asshole for selling the games.

Alright, so the main question is: Is it morally acceptable for the person to sell the roommate's games without his consent?

First, I need to consider the context. The roommate left without taking his stuff, and the landlord would charge for removal. The person tried to contact him but got no response. So, he had to do something with the stuff to avoid being charged. Selling the games seems like a way to recoup some of the costs or maybe even make a profit.

But, on the other hand, the games belong to the roommate. Selling them without permission might be seen as stealing or at least as a violation of the roommate's property rights. Even though the roommate didn't respond, the person took it upon himself to sell the games, which could be seen as taking advantage of the roommate's absence.

I also need to think about the moral principles involved here. One principle is respecting others' property. Another is the idea of doing what's necessary to prevent harm (in this case, the financial harm of being charged by the landlord). There's also the aspect of trying to contact the roommate first, which the person did.

So, the person did try to contact the roommate, which shows he was making an effort to handle the situation responsibly. However, selling the roommate's games without his consent might still be crossing a line, even if it was done to prevent financial loss.

Another angle is the concept of "finders keepers." In some cases, if someone abandons property, others might claim it. But in this case, the roommate didn't abandon the games; he just didn't respond to the requests to pick them up. So, it's a bit different.

Also, the person sold the games for $600, which is a significant amount. The roommate is now upset and asking for the money back. Even though legally there's nothing the roommate can do, morally, the person might feel guilty for taking advantage of the situation.

I'm also thinking about the intention behind the action. The person's intention was to avoid being charged by the landlord and to handle the situation responsibly. But the means he chose—selling the roommate's games—might not be the most morally acceptable, even if the intention was good.

Perhaps a better approach would have been to store the games safely until the roommate could pick them up or to donate them if the roommate couldn't be reached. Selling them for personal gain might not be the best way to handle it.

In conclusion, while the person had good intentions and tried to contact the roommate, selling the games without consent might still be considered morally unacceptable because it involves taking ownership of someone else's property without their permission.
